subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is a hormone?
options: A chemical messenger secreted by a gland and carried in the blood
An electrical impulse carried along a neurone
An enzyme that speeds up digestion in the gut
A protein that carries oxygen around the body
questions.explain: Hormones are chemical messengers made by endocrine glands and transported in the bloodstream to their target organs.

questions.q: Which gland is often described as the 'master gland' because it controls several other endocrine glands?
options: Pituitary gland
Thyroid gland
Adrenal gland
Pancreas
questions.explain: The pituitary gland secretes hormones that act on other endocrine glands, coordinating their activity.

questions.q: How does a hormonal (endocrine) response typically differ from a nervous response?
options: It is generally slower to act but longer lasting
It is generally faster to act but shorter lasting
It uses electrical impulses instead of chemicals
It is always confined to a single target cell only
questions.explain: Hormones travel in the blood, so responses are usually slower to begin but their effects persist for longer than rapid nervous responses.

questions.q: Which hormone, produced by the thyroid gland, controls the body's basal metabolic rate?
options: Thyroxine
Insulin
Adrenaline
Testosterone
questions.explain: Thyroxine is released by the thyroid gland and regulates the rate of metabolism in the body.

questions.q: A student is startled by a loud bang and their heart begins to pound. Which hormone and gland are responsible for this 'fight or flight' response?
options: Adrenaline released by the adrenal glands
Insulin released by the pancreas
Thyroxine released by the thyroid gland
ADH released by the pituitary gland
questions.explain: Adrenaline from the adrenal glands raises heart rate and prepares the body for action in a fight or flight response.

questions.q: Which organ monitors and controls the concentration of glucose in the blood?
options: Pancreas
Liver
Kidney
Stomach
questions.explain: The pancreas detects blood glucose levels and secretes insulin or glucagon to keep them within limits.

questions.q: When blood glucose concentration rises after a meal, insulin is released. What effect does insulin have?
options: It causes body cells to take up glucose and the liver to store it as glycogen
It causes the liver to break down glycogen into glucose
It causes glucose to be released from the muscles into the blood
It stops the pancreas from detecting glucose
questions.explain: Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake into cells and the conversion of excess glucose to glycogen in the liver.

questions.q: When blood glucose concentration falls too low, glucagon is released. What is its role?
options: It makes the liver convert glycogen into glucose, raising blood glucose
It makes cells absorb more glucose, lowering blood glucose
It converts glucose into glycogen for storage
It stimulates the pancreas to release insulin
questions.explain: Glucagon raises blood glucose by stimulating the liver to break down stored glycogen back into glucose.

questions.q: What is the main cause of Type 1 diabetes?
options: The pancreas does not produce enough insulin
The body's cells stop responding to insulin
The liver stores too much glycogen
The kidneys reabsorb too little glucose
questions.explain: In Type 1 diabetes the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin, so it is usually treated with insulin injections.

questions.q: A person has a mass of 90 kg and a height of 1.5 m. Using BMI = mass (kg) / height (m)^2, what is their BMI?
questions.explain: BMI = 90 / (1.5 x 1.5) = 90 / 2.25 = 40, which is a raised value linked to Type 2 diabetes risk.

questions.q: Which part of the brain acts as the thermoregulatory centre, monitoring core body temperature?
options: The hypothalamus
The cerebellum
The medulla
The pituitary gland
questions.explain: The hypothalamus contains the thermoregulatory centre, which detects the temperature of the blood.

questions.q: When the body becomes too hot, which combination of responses helps to cool it down?
options: Vasodilation of skin blood vessels and increased sweating
Vasoconstriction of skin blood vessels and shivering
Shivering and hairs standing on end
Reduced sweating and vasoconstriction
questions.explain: Vasodilation brings more blood near the skin surface to lose heat, while sweat evaporation removes energy from the body.

questions.q: What is the approximate normal core body temperature that thermoregulation maintains in humans?
options: 37 degrees C
30 degrees C
42 degrees C
25 degrees C
questions.explain: Human enzymes work best at around 37 degrees C, so the body maintains this core temperature.

questions.q: A hiker becomes very cold on a mountain. Which set of responses would you expect their body to show?
options: Vasoconstriction of skin blood vessels and shivering
Vasodilation of skin blood vessels and sweating
Increased sweating and hairs lying flat
Vasodilation and shivering together
questions.explain: In the cold, blood vessels constrict to reduce heat loss and muscles shiver to release heat from respiration.

questions.q: How does sweating help to cool the body down?
options: Water in sweat evaporates, transferring energy from the skin to the surroundings
Sweat traps a layer of warm air against the skin
Sweat causes blood vessels to constrict
Sweat is absorbed back into the blood carrying heat away
questions.explain: Evaporation of sweat requires energy, which is taken from the skin, cooling the body.

questions.q: Excess amino acids cannot be stored, so they are broken down in the liver to form urea. What is this breakdown process called?
options: Deamination
Filtration
Reabsorption
Osmosis
questions.explain: Deamination in the liver removes the nitrogen-containing part of excess amino acids, producing urea for excretion.

questions.q: What effect does antidiuretic hormone (ADH) have on the kidney?
options: It increases the amount of water reabsorbed back into the blood
It increases the amount of water lost in the urine
It increases the reabsorption of urea into the blood
It stops the kidney filtering the blood
questions.explain: ADH makes the kidney tubules more permeable so more water is reabsorbed, producing less, more concentrated urine.

questions.q: On a hot day a runner sweats heavily and does not drink. What happens to their ADH secretion and urine?
options: More ADH is released and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced
Less ADH is released and a large volume of dilute urine is produced
More ADH is released and a large volume of dilute urine is produced
ADH secretion stops and no urine is produced
questions.explain: Dehydration makes the blood more concentrated, so more ADH is released to conserve water, giving concentrated urine.

questions.q: Which gland releases antidiuretic hormone (ADH) to help regulate the water content of the blood?
options: Pituitary gland
Adrenal gland
Thyroid gland
Pancreas
questions.explain: ADH is secreted by the pituitary gland in response to changes in blood water concentration detected by the hypothalamus.

questions.q: In the kidney nephron, useful substances such as glucose are removed from the filtrate and returned to the blood. What is this process called?
options: Selective reabsorption
Ultrafiltration
Deamination
Vasoconstriction
questions.explain: After ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption returns all the glucose and needed water and ions from the filtrate back into the blood.
